questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presented with acute vision loss on the left. His eye was not painful. There was no discharge from his eye. He had no past medical history. He reported unprotected sex with 3 male sexual partners in the last 6 months. He had never had an HIV test. On examination there was a posterior uveitis of the left eye. Investigations: Syphilis EIA positive RPR 1:128 FTA-ABS positive HIV test pending
questions.lead_in: What is the next best test?

options.text: Urine nucleic acid amplification testing for Chlamydia

questions.explanation: Lumbar puncture Lumbar puncture (LP) is indicated to evaluate for neurosyphilis if ocular syphilis is present. All patients with ocular syphilis require HIV testing and LP . Neisseria may cause a keratoconjunctivitis and typically has very purulent discharge. Chlamydia may cause conjunctivitis that can progress to keratitis but does not typically cause posterior uveitis. The patient should have pain if the cornea is involved.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q10

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with acute unilateral vision loss. On funduscopic examination, he has significant vitreitis and retinal findings concerning for acute retinal necrosis.
questions.explanation: Aciclovir Acute retinal necrosis is most often caused by varicella zoster virus, and therapy with aciclovir should be administered. Corticosteroids may be used to decrease ocular inflammation but should not be given until after antiviral therapy is initiated.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q30

questions.question: Necrotizing uveitis (acute retinal necrosis).

parts.text: Four anatomic sites of uveitis that would differentiate the etiology

parts_raw.text: 4 anatomic sites of uveitis that would differentiate the etiology

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Varicella-zoster virus (2) Herpes simplex virus - together account for nearly all cases of acute retinal necrosis in immunocompetent hosts (vitreous PCR in 18 HIV-negative ARN patients: VZV 12, HSV 4). CMV is a rare cause, seen in the immunocompromised.
b) (1) Toxoplasma gondii - most common infectious cause of posterior uveitis in the United States, creamy yellow chorioretinal lesion with overlying vitritis (2) Toxocara canis (3) Toxocara cati - ocular toxocariasis in children, presenting as posterior pole granuloma, peripheral granuloma, or diffuse panuveitis.
c) (1) Anterior uveitis - pain, ciliary flush, anterior chamber cells, keratic precipitates, quiet vitreous and normal retina (2) Intermediate uveitis - floaters without pain, quiet aqueous, vitreous cells/snowballs and pars plana snow bank; rarely infectious (3) Posterior uveitis - painless vision loss with retinal/choroidal lesions, vitritis typical of toxoplasmosis, no vitritis typical of CMV retinitis (4) Panuveitis - inflammation of both anterior and posterior segments. The anatomic category limits the likely infectious and noninfectious etiologies.
questions.beyond_mandell: This chapter names only Toxoplasma and Toxocara; other parasitic causes of uveitis (Taenia solium/cysticercosis, Onchocerca volvulus, diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis) are covered in the respective parasitology chapters.

Name the four anatomical categories for uveitis

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Varicella-zoster virus (2) Herpes simplex virus. (CMV is a rare cause, considered in immunocompromised patients.)
b) (1) Anterior uveitis (2) Intermediate uveitis (3) Posterior uveitis (4) Panuveitis - assigned by the ophthalmologist according to the site of greatest inflammation.
c) (1) Toxoplasma gondii (2) Toxocara canis (3) Toxocara cati.

cohort_answer.text: Organisms: HSV, VZV, CMV. Anatomical categories: Anterior; Intermediate; Posterior; Panuveitis. Parasites: Toxoplasma gondii; Toxocara canis; Taenia solium; Acanthamoeba

questions.question: Infectious causes of uveitis.
questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Herpes simplex virus - herpetic anterior uveitis (about 10% of anterior uveitis is herpetic; unilateral, often with sectoral iris atrophy and raised intraocular pressure) and acute retinal necrosis (2) Varicella-zoster virus - anterior uveitis, acute retinal necrosis, and progressive outer retinal necrosis. (Also CMV anterior uveitis/retinitis, dengue, chikungunya, West Nile, Ebola, Zika.)
b) (1) Treponema pallidum - ocular syphilis, uveitis is the commonest manifestation, often granulomatous, any anatomic category; all cases need HIV testing and lumbar puncture (2) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - most commonly focal or multifocal choroiditis/choroidal tubercles, often without evident systemic disease. (Also Bartonella, Borrelia burgdorferi, Brucella, Leptospira, Mycobacterium leprae, Tropheryma whipplei.)

cohort_answer.text:
A) HSV (most common!), VZV, CMV, West Nile, Ebola virus, Zika virus.

B) M. tuberculosis, Bartonella sp., T. pallidum, B. burgdorferi, Brucella.

questions.question: A child presents with unilateral subacute vision loss and hyperemia, with no other details given.
questions.question_raw: Most likely parasitic infection of a child with unilateral subacute vision loss and hyperemia? No other details given

parts.text: Most likely way to make the diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: C) Most likely way to make the dx?

questions.model_answer: a) Diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN) caused by a migrating subretinal nematode; the usual culprits are Ancylostoma caninum (smaller worm, southeastern US) and Baylisascaris procyonis (larger worm, raccoon roundworm) — ocular toxocariasis (Toxocara canis) is the other main consideration. b) (1) Laser photocoagulation of the worm once it is directly visualized on fundoscopy (definitive). (2) Oral anthelmintic therapy — albendazole (often with a corticosteroid to control the inflammatory/vision loss component). c) Dilated fundoscopic (ophthalmoscopic) examination to identify the motile subretinal nematode.
questions.beyond_mandell: DUSN diagnosis/treatment details (fundoscopy, laser photocoagulation, albendazole) are from ophthalmology/parasitology literature (Gass; Mandell references 19-21); the DUSN body text is not in the provided page slice.

cohort_answer.text:
Ancylostoma caninum (southern US); Baylisascaris procyonis (Midwest, northwest US). DDx: Toxoplasmosis, Toxocara canis, Gnathostoma spinigerum, Strongyloides stercoralis, Brugia malayi
Albendazole 400mg/day x30 days; Prednisone taper due to vision loss; Photocoagulation if worm visualized
Fundoscopic exam
